title.narrative: Protecting the rights of children in the coconut oil supply chain in the Philippines

description.narrative: In the smallholder coconut farms in the Philippines, children are often at risk of becoming part of the labour force, a reality driven by poverty, lack of access to education. With support from the Fund against Child Labour (FBK), a pioneering project set out to change this by bringing together farmers, communities, companies, and government institutions in a united effort to protect children from exploitative labour in the sector.At the heart of the initiative was the creation of a Child Labour Monitoring and Remediation System (CLMRS), a community-based mechanism that now enables local authorities to systematically identify and respond to potential child labour cases. Over the course of the project, numerous children were profiled, resulting in the identification of several child labour cases. These children were directly referred to the Department of Labour and Employment, the Department of Social Welfare and Development, and schools to ensure education and protection support. Some were reintegrated into formal schooling, others enrolled in alternative learning systems, and families received food and livelihood assistance to help ease the economic pressures that drive child labour. Barangay (in the Philippines, a small territorial and administrative district forming the most local level of government) Councils for the Protection of Children and local helpdesks were also strengthened, ensuring that monitoring continues long after the project’s end.Protecting children also meant addressing the root causes of the problem. Farmers were trained in good agricultural practices, and connected to welfare schemes and support programs from the Philippines Coconut Authority and Department of Trade and Industry. These measures not only improved incomes but also built resilience against the shocks that so often push families to rely on child labour. The two companies involved in the project, Cargill and Wilmar, set up internal technical working groups focusing on child protection, assessed existing supplier management frameworks and HRDD mechanisms to identify potential gaps and strengths, and began training suppliers on child labour due diligence. This pilot project demonstrates that change begins with collective action. By coming together to explore solutions and share insights, these companies have shown willingness to address complex challenges like child labour. Additionally, it is worth noting that the local government aims to achieve child-friendly local governance, a crucial mandatory component to earn the Seal of Good Local Governance (SGLG). To qualify, LGUs (local government units) must meet criteria focused on Child Survival, Development, Protection, Participation, and Governance. The benefit for local governments includes access to development funds and opportunities for continuous improvement, leading to better and more efficient service delivery to citizens. Additionally, the Child Labor Monitoring and Remediation System (CLMRS) supports the social protection criteria, helping LGUs qualify for the SGLG.The journey was not without obstacles. The devastating 2023–24 El Niño and a powerful earthquake disrupted farming, reduced yields, and strained livelihoods. Yet the resilience built through training, support services, and stronger safety nets allowed communities to weather the crisis and continue protecting their children.Another added value of the project is the way it has introduced child labour monitoring into the fabric of community governance, farmer welfare systems, and company operations. By creating a framework of lessons and practical guidance shaped with valuable input from the companies themselves, the project offers a tool that can guide similar efforts in other commodities and countries. In showing how grassroots action, farmer empowerment, and collaborative industry efforts can reinforce one another.
